name: Elena Walsh

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for a side. Your answers are confidential. What's an ordinary shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate blast-hole drills at Granite Flats, a large iron ore mine. I check the drilling pattern, spend part of the week in a cab, and spend two shifts watching remotely controlled drills from town. I like working out why a bit of ground fights the bit. The long drive and the cab's shaking are harder on my back now.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What sits behind work when you go home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sam, my husband, runs a small café, and we've got two children, Ruby and Finn, both in school. The mortgage is there, but we have more than six months of expenses saved and my mine pay is good. There are other mines within reach if I had to move jobs. I did a vocational certificate, and I use an AI assistant every day for shift notes and checking drill data.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the grand promises have settled into a handy report writer. I'd still ask for money to go toward safer cabs and proper training. A tidy shift note isn't worth a sore back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a little disappointed because I enjoy learning the software. But the drill still needs me, the pay cheque stays, and our mortgage is manageable. My AI habit would remain useful even if the big story fizzled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my two remote shifts and use the assistant to check my shift notes against the drill logs. I'd keep our monthly transfer to the index fund and leave Sam's café budget alone. In the first year I'd ask the safety representative to raise the cab seats again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, with a bit of impatience. I can live with a boring future if the cab stops rattling my spine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the remote work matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me finish a week without lying flat all Saturday. The mine might change the roster, but I would ask to keep those two shifts. My back is the quiet part of this story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the café be affected?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would still buy flour and pay staff as usual. We would keep a good cash reserve for the café rather than guess about new machines. Its weekend trade matters more to us than a new app.

say: I would call AI a **report helper**, then ask for safer drill cabs and decent training.
I would tell the crew my **remote shifts** still matter more than a clever new promise.
think: I would feel **secure** because the drilling work, pay and family savings remain in place.
I would miss the **learning curve**, even while enjoying shorter reports and fewer errors.
do: Keep **two remote shifts** and check each drill log with the assistant during the first year.
Continue the **monthly fund transfer** and ask the safety representative to revisit cab seats.
feel: **Calm**, with a little impatience about the same old cab pain.
S0.quote: A tidy shift note isn't worth a sore back.
fieldNote: Her **back pain** matters more than the novelty of AI when shifts still run as before.
Her **strong cushion** and other nearby mines make a flat technology path financially comfortable.

steps.text: Keep two remote drill shifts and check each shift log
Continue monthly transfers to the family index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union should bargain for paid training and a place for current drillers in the remote centre. The software may do reports and schedules first; that doesn't mean a robot is holding the drill tomorrow. I'd tell Hugh, my fellow driller, that he deserves a chance to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paperwork side of my job might shrink, and the remote centre might run with fewer people. I'm quick with new systems, so I could be kept, but I can't count on it. I worry more about Hugh, who hates the screen work and has a mortgage too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd enroll in the mine's automation technician course, if the company keeps offering it. In the first year I'd ask the union branch to negotiate paid time for that course and invite Hugh to two practice shifts. I'd also keep our household reserve above six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because I can see the headcount changing, even if I have a route to another role. It feels odd to enjoy a tool and count the chairs it removes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hugh at lunch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say, Hugh, give me two shifts at the remote console before you dismiss it. He knows the sound of a drill better than I do, and I could use that knowledge too. I would not call him backward.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would paid time change for the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A course after a twelve-hour shift is an empty offer. The union should bargain for scheduled hours on the clock. I would be at that meeting, with the course timetable in my hand.

say: I would ask the **union** to secure paid training and remote posts for current drillers.
I would explain that **reports and schedules** change before a robot replaces a person at the controls.
think: I could keep a role through **new skills**, but fewer remote operators may still be needed.
I worry Hugh could be **left behind** despite knowing the drill better than I do.
do: Enroll in the **technician course** this month if the mine still offers it.
Bring a **paid training** proposal to the union and offer Hugh two console practice shifts.
feel: **Uneasy** about a smaller team, though another role feels possible.
S1.quote: A course after a twelve-hour shift is an empty offer.
fieldNote: Her **early adoption** gives her a route into equipment work but no guarantee of a retained seat.
Her **union proposal** turns concern for colleagues into paid hours and a specific course.

steps.text: Enroll in the mine automation technician course this month if offered
Ask the union branch for paid training hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2028 would hit the planning room before it hits the pit. The union should demand a share of any savings and paid retraining now. I would tell the crew that robot drills on the card come around 2031, and three years is a short runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028 the system could plan patterns, read faults and write reports better than I can. My hands-on cab work could last until around 2031, but the remote team could thin sooner. Savings and other mines buy us choices, yet I could lose the higher pay that carries our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move part of our monthly investment contribution into a separate cash reserve now, after talking with Sam. In the first year after 2028 I'd apply for maintenance shifts that still need hands on the machines and finish any course I can. I'd bring a written request for paid redeployment to the union meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and quite angry that the planning side could vanish so fast. I'm not helpless, but I don't want our children learning about layoffs at the dinner table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What amount would you put in cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would aim for another three months of mortgage and groceries in cash before buying more fund units. Sam and I would decide the amount together. The café can have a slow season, so I cannot treat its income as guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Ruby and Finn, our children, that my job may change and we have money set aside. I would wait until the roster actually shifts before mentioning a lost job. They need the truth, not my worst guess.

say: I would say **planning work** could go by 2028, while comparable hands-on robots follow around 2031.
I would push the **union** for paid redeployment and a share of savings before the drill roster shrinks.
think: I could lose **remote hours** early and higher pay later, even with savings and other mines nearby.
I would count the café as **uncertain income** because a slow season could coincide with a mine cut.
do: Shift part of the **fund contribution** into a three-month cash target after discussing it with Sam.
Apply for **maintenance shifts** after 2028 and seek paid redeployment through the union branch.
feel: **Anxious** about the mortgage and children, but able to form a plan.
S2.quote: I don't want our children learning about layoffs at the dinner table.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 planning changes** from the hands-on robot risk around 2031.
Her **cash target** adds three months of costs; it does not assume café income will rescue the household.
She seeks **maintenance shifts** and union backed redeployment while she still has work.

steps.text: Build another three months of mortgage and grocery cash
Apply for hands-on mine maintenance shifts after 2028
Request paid redeployment at the union branch meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to negotiate a fair transition. Pattern planning may go in 2031, but hands-on robot capability follows around 2034. I would put that timing on the union noticeboard so nobody confuses the two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let me finish the technician course and work in maintenance while the mine changes. But by 2034 even that work could be under pressure, so I cannot sell it to myself as a permanent shelter. I would still be paying the mortgage, with two teenagers at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd complete the first course module and ask the maintenance lead for a trial shift. I'd keep the family cash reserve intact and direct any extra bonus into the mortgage. In the first year after 2031 I'd seek a maintenance contract at this or another nearby mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less rushed than in the 2028 picture. I can make a real move before the planning work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the maintenance lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask to spend one paid shift tracing a drill fault beside a fitter. I know the machine from the operator seat, not from inside the panel. The trial would tell me whether I could do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you open a second café with Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Sam can show steady takings at the first café and enough cash for a bad year. I would not borrow against the house just to escape a forecast. The children still need somewhere secure to live.

say: I would mark **2031** for planning changes and **2034** for hands-on robot capability on the union board.
I would ask for a **fair transition** while experienced drillers still have time to qualify.
think: A **maintenance role** could bridge several years, yet robots might threaten that work around 2034.
Our **mortgage** still matters even with a sizeable reserve and nearby mine vacancies.
do: Finish the **first course module** this year and request a paid maintenance trial shift.
Put any **extra bonus** toward the mortgage and seek nearby maintenance work after 2031.
feel: **Anxious**, though five years gives a usable preparation window.
S3.quote: I would not borrow against the house just to escape a forecast.
fieldNote: She treats **training** as a bridge into machine maintenance rather than a guaranteed permanent answer.
The **mortgage decision** shows a limit to her appetite for risk despite her curiosity about technology.

steps.text: Finish the first automation course module this year
Put any extra mine bonus toward the mortgage
Seek maintenance work at this or another nearby mine after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is long enough to make paid retraining real, if we start early. AGI by 2036 could take the planning work, with hands-on robots arriving around 2039. I'd press our union branch to publish a training path each year, not just a speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when the thinking side changes, and the children would be older. I could move into maintenance or remote safety work well before then. I still do not know what either job looks like once hands-on robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enroll in the technician certificate this year, finish it within two years, then ask for paid maintenance rotations. I'd keep investing each month and help Sam test whether the café could afford one more employee, without borrowing against the house. In the first year after 2036 I'd compare safety and maintenance vacancies across the nearby mines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. A decade means I can work through a change instead of just running from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to publish?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want actual course places, paid hours, and a list of jobs graduates obtained. If the mine promises a path, it should show where the path leads. I would help gather the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who might still struggle with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hugh, my fellow driller, might put it off because the current cab still pays well. I would keep offering practice, but I cannot choose for him. I would ask the branch to make training easy to enter at any age.

say: I would push for **paid course places** and yearly reports showing which drillers found new roles.
I would explain the **2036 and 2039** sequence so the crew can plan for both changes.
think: I have time to **qualify** and work in another mine role before the thinking work changes.
I remain unsure whether **maintenance** will hold after hands-on robots arrive around 2039.
do: Enroll in the **technician certificate** this year, then ask for paid maintenance rotations once qualified.
Continue **monthly investing** and check nearby mine vacancies after 2036.
feel: **Uneasy**, but hopeful that a long runway makes a career move possible.
S4.quote: If the mine promises a path, it should show where the path leads.
fieldNote: The **ten-year window** allows a qualification and work experience before the 2036 planning shift.
She demands **course outcomes** from the mine and union rather than trusting a training promise alone.
Her **investment plan** continues because the household can afford a measured transition.

steps.text: Enroll in the mine technician certificate this year
Continue monthly transfers into the family index fund
Compare safety and maintenance vacancies at nearby mines after 2036
Ask the union branch to publish course places and job outcomes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the pattern planning could change almost at once and the drill jobs could follow by 2031. Paid redeployment, real maintenance places and a union agreement to share the mine's savings would help. Our own reserve buys time, but it cannot create a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether liking the tools makes me feel disloyal. I enjoy using them, and I still want the people who taught me to drill to have a future here. I don't think those feelings cancel each other out.

headlineQuote: Our own reserve buys time, but it cannot create a job.
portrait: **Elena Walsh**, 43, operates blast-hole drills at a large iron ore mine and spends two shifts each week at remote controls.
She has **good pay**, more than six months saved, a mortgage, two school-age children and other mines within reach.
A **daily AI user**, she enjoys learning software but worries that leaner remote teams could cost colleagues their jobs.
She pursues **technical training**, cash protection and union bargaining, with the fastest AGI timeline posing the sharpest household risk.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove pattern planning quickly and put hands-on drill roles at risk around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid redeployment**, real maintenance places and a union agreement to share mine savings would give her a practical route.
